title: Carl Sagan: The Pale Blue Dot in the Sunbeam
source_book: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space
authenticity_note: Based on Carl Sagan's campaign to command Voyager 1 to turn its camera backward on February 14, 1990, capturing the famous portrait of Earth from 3.7 billion miles (6 billion km).
summary: As Voyager 1 completed its primary mission and sped toward interstellar space in 1990, astronomer Carl Sagan convinced NASA to turn the spacecraft's camera around. In a beam of scattered sunlight sat Earth—a fragile 'pale blue dot' just 0.12 pixel in size—giving humanity its most profound lesson in humility and planetary brotherhood.
content:
On February 14, 1990, NASA's *Voyager 1* spacecraft had completed its historic grand tour of the outer planets. Having visited Jupiter and Saturn, it was cruising at 40,000 miles per hour toward interstellar space, roughly 3.7 billion miles (6 billion kilometers) away from Earth—beyond the orbit of Neptune.

Astronomer and science communicator Carl Sagan, a member of the Voyager imaging team, made a bold and unconventional request. He asked NASA flight controllers to command the spacecraft to turn its cameras backward for one final look toward home, to capture a 'family portrait' of the solar system before its cameras were turned off forever to conserve power.

Many engineers objected. Pointing the camera so close to the blazing Sun could fry the sensitive vidicon optics. Furthermore, from such an unimaginable distance, Earth would be a meaningless microscopic speck. But Sagan persisted, arguing that this picture would hold deep philosophical and educational power for generations to come.

NASA agreed. Voyager fired its thrusters, rotated, and clicked a mosaic of sixty frames.

When the digital data beamed back across millions of miles, one frame captured the imagination of the world. In the middle of a scattered ray of sunlight reflected off the camera baffle lay a lonely speck of dust—Earth, occupying a mere 0.12 of a single pixel, glowing with a soft, pale blue hue due to sunlight scattering in its oceans and atmosphere.

Sagan penned words that will echo through human history:
*"Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives... every king and peasant, every young couple in love... every corrupt politician, every superstar, every supreme leader, every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there—on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam."*

Sagan noted that there is no hint that help will come from elsewhere to save us from ourselves; it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we have ever known.

stem_vocabulary.definition: A photograph of planet Earth taken on February 14, 1990, by the Voyager 1 space probe from a record distance of about 6 billion kilometers.
The collective ethical obligation of humanity to preserve and protect the living biosphere of Earth.
The scattering of light by particles much smaller than the wavelength of the light, causing Earth's ocean and atmospheric blueness.
The physical space within a galaxy not occupied by stars or their planetary systems.
